chunks: Why PCBs are green; other colours. The question: Why are PCBs often green? What other colors could they be?
The color of a circuit board is the color of its soldermask, the thin coating over the copper. The fiberglass underneath is a pale tan.
Green is the default because it is the oldest, cheapest and best-tuned coating, and it is easy to inspect. Other colors work the same electrically.
They just trade away some cost, visibility or convenience.
Think of a car's paint. Red paint and gray paint do not change how the engine runs. But a dark color can hide a scratch that a light color would show. A board is the same.
The coating color changes nothing about the circuit, but black hides traces and solder problems from your eyes and from inspection cameras.
The analogy breaks in one place: a car paint choice rarely affects how readable its labels are, while a board's text color must contrast with the mask.
The same mini board (a trace, two pads and a legend) over six mask colours.
Notice how the trace (the mask over copper appears lighter) is clearly visible on green, red, blue and yellow, is low-contrast on white, and almost vanishes on black.
The legend needs the right colour too: white text on green, red, blue and black; black text on white and yellow.
Soldermask: the polymer coating over the copper that sets the board color ("What soldermask is and does").
Contrast: how clearly features such as traces and text stand out against the mask. AOI (automated optical inspection): cameras that check boards, usually tuned to green.
Silkscreen: the printed text layer on top, which needs the right color against the mask ("The silkscreen (legend) layer").
Laminate: the fiberglass-epoxy board underneath, which is not the colored part ("PCB layers and their materials").
Order two identical prototypes, one green and one black. Electrically they behave the same. Now one trace is cut by mistake.
On the green board you can see the trace and the cut under a lamp. On the black board the trace almost vanishes, so you hunt longer.
White text works on green but not on a white mask, which needs black text.
So use green while developing, and pick a colored mask for the final product only if the look is worth the harder inspection. That is the whole idea.
"The colour is the soldermask, the polymer coating over the copper, not the fibreglass.
Green is the default because it's the most mature and cheapest mask chemistry, it gives good contrast with copper and white silkscreen, it's easy on the eyes, and inspection systems are tuned to it.
There's also some military-spec folklore.

Other colours, red, blue, black, white, yellow, work electrically the same: black looks premium but hides traces and makes debugging harder, white is good for LED reflectivity, and the rest are cosmetic."
